prose:gloss-dual-practice:
Dual practice.

Term: Dual practice.

Status: open. 3 candidate definitions, none adopted.

Candidate 1 (WHO. Health practitioner regulation: design, reform and implementation guidance. 2024):

Phenomenon in which a health practitioner is simultaneously employed or holds dual or multiple appointments (in both the public and private sectors) in regulated as well as unregulated ways and in an authorized or informal manner.

Candidate 2 (WHO. National health workforce accounts: a handbook, 2nd ed. 2023):

Multiple health-related practices by a health worker in the same or different sites. Dual practice in this sense may be public-on-public, public-on-private, or private-on-private.

Candidate 3 (WHO. Health labour market analysis guidebook. 2021):

There are several forms of dual practice. Health professionals can work in a public service provision role and another role: (a) outside: in a completely separate private environment; (b) beside: in a private ward or clinic physically associated with a public facility but run as a separate business; (c) within: where private services are offered inside a public facility but outside public service operating hours or space; or (d) integrated: where additional fees are charged for services offered alongside standard public ones, often informally, on the understanding of a faster – or higher-quality – service. Academics and policy-makers typically restrict the term dual practice to category (a), but it is clear that categories (b), (c) and (d) present alternative scenarios for health professionals to combine public and private practice, and supplement public sector salaries; policy-making in this domain should navigate the trade-offs between the objective of retaining personnel while ensuring their commitment to public sector objectives (15)

prose:gloss-education-and-training-insti:
Education and training institution (Health workforce).

Term: Education and training institution (Health workforce).

Status: open. 1 candidate definition, none adopted.

Candidate 1 (WHO. National health workforce accounts: a handbook, 2nd ed. 2023):

An established institution that provides education as its main purpose, such as a school, college, university or training centre. Such institutions are normally accredited or sanctioned by the relevant national education authorities or equivalent to award qualifications. Educational institutions may also be operated by private organizations, such as religious bodies, special interest groups or private educational and training enterprises, both for-profit and not-for-profit. Types of health workforce education and training institutions are: • Public: Public educational institutions provide core educational services such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres. They are controlled and managed directly by a public education authority or governing body (council, committee, etc.), the majority of whose members are appointed by a public authority. • Private: Private educational institutions provide core educational products such as teaching activities and ancillary services. They include schools, colleges, universities, and training centres, that are controlled and directly managed either by a private organization such as a church, trade union, or business enterprise, or by a governing board whose members have mostly not been selected by a public authority. Whether or not an institution is private is therefore a matter of management, not funding. A school, for example, could in theory be entirely publicly funded but still be considered private because it is not managed by the government. In practice, for international comparability, any educational institution not managed by a government institution is classified as private.
prose:gloss-employment-status-full-time-:
Employment status: full-time, part-time, temporary, permanent.

Term: Employment status: full-time, part-time, temporary, permanent.

Status: open. 1 candidate definition, none adopted.

Candidate 1 (WHO. Health labour market analysis guidebook. 2021):

Full-time (whole-time) is employment for or working for the amount of time considered customary or standard. Part-time is employment for or working for less than the amount of time considered customary or standard. Permanent is employment contracted for an indeterminate period. Fixed term is employment contracted for a fixed period of time. Temporary refers to short-term contracts or “casual” work, either for a definite period or for a specific activity. Self-employment is when remuneration is directly dependent upon the profits derived from the goods and services produced by the individual.

The dynamic between the number and the kind of jobs offered on the market and the number of health workers is central in determining the configuration of the health labour market

prose:gloss-health-workforce:
Health workforce (HWF).

Status: open. 1 candidate definition, none adopted.

Candidate 1 (WHO AFRO. Africa Health Workforce Investment Charter):

All people engaged in actions whose primary intent is to enhance health. They may be paid staff or volunteers working full-time or part-time in the public and private sectors. They may be delivering health services, managing the services offered by the system, or addressing social determinants of health. That means that the health workforce includes: all personnel trained in health occupations delivering clinical work in health facilities (such as medical doctors, nurses, or dentists); all non health professionals employed in the health sector, public and private, regardless of their occupation (such as managers, ambulance drivers or teachers of health education); and all those whose work supports the delivery of health services, even if they are employed by other sectors or industries (such as cleaning, catering, security or agency staff working in the health sector)
prose:gloss-health-workforce-observatory:
Health workforce observatory.

Also: HRH observatory (national).

Status: open. 4 candidate definitions, none adopted.

Candidate 1 (WHO AFRO. Regional framework for Workforce 2030. 2020):

A Health Workforce Observatory is a platform or mechanism for generating, analyzing, sharing, and using human resources for health (HRH) data and evidence to support policy-making, planning, monitoring, and research. The African Regional Framework describes national health workforce observatories as platforms for generating and sharing HRH data and best practices and notes that workforce observatories support evidence-based policies

Candidate 2 (WHO. Strengthening the collection, analysis and use of health workforce data and information. 2022):

Where they exist, HRH observatories are an excellent governance platform for the coordination of NHWA implementation. These observatories can be expanded and adapted to align progressively with NHWA implementation principles and requirements.” Page: 259 “In the WHO African, Americas and South-East Asia regions, several countries mutualize forces through HRH observatories to collect, analyse and disseminate health workforce data. These initiatives resulted from understanding that no single organization or body can compile all the relevant health workforce indicators without overburdening countries and duplicating efforts already conducted by others.” Page: 263

Candidate 3 (WHO. Human resources for health observatories. 2012):

There is no consensual definition of what an observatory is. There are various ways and means to achieve the same goals and objectives, and no blue-print or “best practice” can be prescribed (Hemmings, Wilkinson 2003). In the social sector, these organizations go beyond observing and analysing; they also pro-actively intervene on the reality, which they monitor. The simple activity of data and information-gathering and dissemination has effects on the reality of the sector and on the actors’ behaviours. HRH observatories are no exception, and in this sense they are rather more like independent policy think-tanks. It is therefore important to note first that there are various “types” of HRH observatory, which take different forms depending on when they were established, by whom, where they are located organizationally, what functions and activities they perform, which resources and funding sources they have, and on the actors involved in their development and management. Table 1 presents that variety of types of observatories according to a number of significant dimensions.

Candidate 4 (OpenHIE Health Worker Registry implementation guide (IntraHealth/CapacityPlus, 2016)):

A cooperative organization designed to promote, develop and sustain a knowledge base for human resources for health in a region or country. It provides evidence for policy decisions to strengthen health systems and improve health service delivery."

EMR Pakistan Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PMDC) Medicine and dentistry The statutory regulatory authority maintaining the official register of medical and dental practitioners in Pakistan, most recently re-established under the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council Act, 2022, after a 2019-2023 period during which its functions were held by the short-lived Pakistan Medical Commission. (Nursing is regulated separately — see the Pakistan Nursing Council row added below.) Sets minimum qualification and education standards for medicine and dentistry jointly with the Higher Education Commission; requires registration of all practitioners and students before legal practice; administers the national licensing/registration examination and register. Pakistan Medical and Dental Council Act, 2022; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Medical_and_Dental_Council; https://pmdc.pk/Documents/law/PMDC%20Act.pdf
EMR Pakistan Pakistan Nursing Council (PNC) / Pakistan Nursing and Midwifery Council (PNMC) Nursing, midwifery, lady health visitors (LHVs) and nursing auxiliaries Pakistan's statutory nursing regulator, founded 1948 with statutory authority under the Pakistan Nursing Council Act (1952, revised 1973); more recently operating as the Pakistan Nursing and Midwifery Council (PNMC) — the exact current legal name/statute in force should be confirmed against Pakistan's official gazette given the same period of institutional flux that affected PMDC. Licenses nurses, midwives, lady health visitors and nursing auxiliaries to practise throughout Pakistan; accredited by, and coordinates nursing education quality assurance with, the Higher Education Commission. Pakistan Nursing Council Act (1952, rev. 1973); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Nursing_Council; https://pnmc.gov.pk/
EMR Egypt Egyptian Medical Syndicate (EMS) Medicine A semi-governmental professional syndicate founded in 1940, with mandatory membership required for physicians to practise. Sources consulted give conflicting founding/governing law numbers, so the precise statutory citation should be confirmed against the Egyptian Official Gazette before use in the handbook. (Nursing is regulated separately by its own syndicate — see the row added below.) Assists the Ministry of Health in conferring licences to physicians; verifies academic credentials on application and issues practice certificates; administers licence renewals and approval of foreign-trained doctors; since February 2021 shares national licensing-exam administration with the newly created Egyptian Health Council for new graduates. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_Medical_Syndicate; https://grokipedia.com/page/egyptian_medical_syndicate (law citation unverified — flagged)
EMR Egypt Nursing Professions Syndicate Nursing A mandatory professional syndicate for Egyptian nurses, distinct from the Egyptian Medical Syndicate, operating under Law No. 155 of 1976 (Official Gazette, 9 November 1976). Membership is mandatory to legally practise nursing in Egypt; the syndicate's Registration Committee verifies nursing credentials and the Ministry of Health-issued practice licence before granting membership, with appeal rights through the syndicate's Council and ultimately the Administrative Court. Law No. 155/1976; https://nazra.org/en/2013/12/q-about-law-regulation-nursing-professions-syndicate
EMR Jordan Jordan Medical Council (JMC) Medicine A body with its own legal personality and financial/administrative independence, headed by the Minister of Health, established under Jordanian medical council legislation approved by parliament in 2022. Note: the precise official statute number/gazette citation should be verified directly with JMC or the Jordanian Official Gazette before use in the handbook. (Nursing is regulated separately — see the Jordanian Nursing Council row added below.) Verifies medical credentials of Jordanian and foreign-trained doctors; administers (or grants defined exemptions from) the Jordanian licensing examination; grants physicians the legal privilege to practise medicine in Jordan; sets category-based registration requirements. 2022 Jordan Medical Council law, as reported by Jordan Times; https://jordantimes.com/news/local/lower-house-approves-2022-jordanian-medical-council-draft-law; https://dataflowgroup.com/organization/jordan-medical-council/
EMR Jordan Jordanian Nursing Council (JNC) Nursing and midwifery A government institution with administrative and financial independence responsible for regulating the nursing profession in Jordan, first established by temporary legislation in 2002 and formalized permanently under Law No. 53 of 2006. Regulates and advances the nursing and midwifery professions, alongside the separate Jordan Medical Council for physicians; develops nursing human resources and supports scientific research; contributes to national health-strategy implementation and protects public health. Law No. 53 of 2006; https://jnc.gov.jo/En/Pages/JNC_Establishment__
EMR Lebanon Lebanese Order of Physicians (LOP) Medicine The statutory professional order for physicians in Lebanon, operating under Law No. 1658 of 17 January 1979 regulating the practice of the medical profession (Official Gazette, Issue 10, 8 March 1979). (Nursing is regulated separately — see the Order of Nurses in Lebanon row added below.) Determines physicians' professional eligibility to practise medicine; disciplines members against professional and ethical rules; advises government ministries on health-workforce laws and regulations; administers retirement and welfare funds for members. Law No. 1658 (1979); https://lopbeirut.org/en/law-regulating-the-practice-of-the-medical-profession-in-lebanon/; https://lopbeirut.org/en/lop-role/
EMR Lebanon Order of Nurses in Lebanon (ONL) Nursing A mandatory regulatory body for Lebanon's nursing profession, established in 2002 and comprising all qualified nurses holding licences issued by the Lebanese Ministry of Public Health; distinct from the Lebanese Order of Physicians, which regulates only medicine. Regulates nursing practice and maintains professional standards; registers and recognizes nurses licensed by the Ministry of Public Health, ensuring only qualified practitioners are authorized to work; works to strengthen patient safety and community health outcomes. Established 2002; https://www.icn.ch/membership/our-members/order-nurses-lebanon-onl
EMR Qatar Department of Healthcare Professions (DHP), Ministry of Public Health All licensed healthcare practitioners, including medicine and nursing (single omnibus regulator) The sole regulatory authority for healthcare practitioners in Qatar, created by Emiri Decree No. 14 of 2019 restructuring the Ministry of Public Health and absorbing the former Qatar Council for Healthcare Practitioners (established by Emiri Decree No. 7 of 2013, building on Law No. 13 of 2002); regulates both medicine and nursing as a single omnibus body. Registers and licenses healthcare practitioners as the sole authority for the state; operates a Fitness to Practise function for complaints and ethical compliance; sets accreditation standards for medical education and continuing professional development. Emiri Decree No. 14 (2019); https://dhp.moph.gov.qa/en/Pages/AboutUs.aspx
EMR Saudi Arabia Saudi Commission for Health Specialties (SCFHS) All licensed health professions, including medicine and nursing (single omnibus regulator) A Saudi professional scientific commission with an independent legal personality, established by Royal Order No. M/2 of 1992 and supervised by a Board of Trustees; functions as a single omnibus regulator covering medicine, nursing, and other health professions rather than separate profession-specific councils. Classifies and registers health practitioners by professional rank through its Professional Practice Executive Board; accredits training programmes and healthcare specialties; sets and enforces continuing professional development and re-licensing requirements. Royal Order No. M/2 (1992); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Commission_for_Health_Specialties
EMR United Arab Emirates (Dubai) Dubai Health Authority (DHA) All licensed health professions, including medicine and nursing (single omnibus regulator for Dubai) A public authority with independent legal personality established under Law No. (6) of 2018 Concerning the Dubai Health Authority (superseding the 2007 law that first created it); one of three UAE healthcare regulators alongside the federal Ministry of Health and Prevention (MOHAP, Northern Emirates) and the Abu Dhabi Department of Health (DoH) — the UAE has no single national medical or nursing council, and DHA licenses both doctors and nurses as a single omnibus regulator for Dubai. Authorises individuals and facilities to practise health professions in Dubai and issues professional licences; sets bylaws, standards and requirements for practice; audits and inspects practitioners and facilities for compliance; investigates complaints and alleged malpractice. Law No. (6) of 2018 Concerning the Dubai Health Authority; https://dlp.dubai.gov.ae/Legislation%20Reference/2018/Law%20No.%20(6)%20of%202018%20Concerning%20the%20Dubai%20Health%20Authority.html; https://alkabban.com/medical-law/healthcare-regulatory-authorities-uae/
EUR Ireland Medical Council of Ireland Medicine Ireland's statutory regulator for the medical profession, originally established by the Medical Practitioners Act 1978 and now operating under the Medical Practitioners Act 2007. Maintains the publicly searchable register of all medical practitioners in Ireland; sets requirements for undergraduate, intern and postgraduate medical education; makes continuing professional development a legal duty (since 2011); specifies conduct/ethics standards and investigates complaints. Medical Practitioners Act 2007; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_Council_of_Ireland
EUR Ireland Nursing and Midwifery Board of Ireland (NMBI) Nursing and midwifery The statutory regulatory body for nurses and midwives in Ireland, governed by the Nurses and Midwives Act 2011. Protects the public and the integrity of the nursing and midwifery professions; maintains the Register of Nurses and Midwives and a Candidate Register for students; sets standards for and approves education/training programmes; investigates fitness-to-practise complaints and imposes sanctions; advises the Minister for Health on nursing/midwifery matters. Nurses and Midwives Act 2011
EUR United Kingdom General Medical Council (GMC) Medicine The statutory regulator for doctors (and, since 2024, physician associates and anaesthesia associates) in the UK, operating under the Medical Act 1983 as amended, most recently by the Anaesthesia Associates and Physician Associates Order 2024. Sets the professional standards doctors must meet; approves and monitors medical education and training; determines eligibility for and maintains the register of licensed doctors (registration plus a licence to practise); investigates fitness-to-practise concerns affecting patient safety. Medical Act 1983; https://www.gmc-uk.org/about/what-we-do-and-why/our-mandate; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Medical_Council
EUR United Kingdom Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC) 15 allied health and other health/care professions (does not cover doctors or nurses/midwives) A statutory corporation and regulatory body established under the Health Professions Order 2001 to protect the public across 15 professions (allied health and other health/care professions; does not cover doctors or nurses/midwives, who are regulated separately — see the GMC and NMC-UK rows added below). Enforces protected professional titles by law; approves qualifying education programs; sets and assesses the baseline Standards of Proficiency and Conduct. Health Professions Order 2001
EUR United Kingdom Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) Nursing, midwifery and nursing associates The statutory regulator for nurses, midwives and nursing associates across the UK, established under the Nursing and Midwifery Order 2001 (in force April 2002), replacing the former UK Central Council for Nursing, Midwifery and Health Visiting. Maintains the register of nurses, midwives, specialist community public health nurses and nursing associates (over 788,000 registrants as of March 2025); sets and reviews education and training standards; investigates fitness-to-practise concerns. Nursing and Midwifery Order 2001; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nursing_and_Midwifery_Council
SEAR India Indian Nursing Council (INC) Nursing An autonomous statutory body formed by the Government of India under the Indian Nursing Council Act, 1947 (Act No. 48 of 1947), operating under the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare alongside the National Medical Commission. Registers nurses at the national level (including via the Nurses Registration & Tracking System, a live national registry); standardizes nursing curricula; recognizes and inspects nursing education institutions; sets professional-compliance standards. Indian Nursing Council Act, 1947; https://www.indiannursingcouncil.org/uploads/inc-act-1947.pdf; https://testbook.com/ugc-net-paper-1/indian-nursing-council
SEAR India National Medical Commission (NMC) Medicine (allopathic) An apex statutory body constituted by an Act of Parliament known as the National Medical Commission Act, 2019. Enforces uniform standards for undergraduate and postgraduate medical education; maintains the National Register; coordinates with State Medical Councils; administers licensing examinations. National Medical Commission Act, 2019
WPR Malaysia Malaysian Medical Council (MMC) Medicine A statutory council established under Part II of the Medical Act 1971 (Act 50), which consolidated and amended the law relating to registration and practice of medical practitioners in Malaysia. (Nursing is regulated separately — see the Nursing Board Malaysia row added below.) Maintains the Register of Medical Practitioners under Part III of the Act; approves qualifications recognized for registration; oversees provisional and full registration, including compulsory post-registration public service; enforces professional conduct standards. Medical Act 1971 (Act 50); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_Act_1971; https://mmc.gov.my/laws-regulations/
WPR Malaysia Nursing Board Malaysia (Lembaga Jururawat Malaysia) Nursing (a separate Midwives Board regulates midwifery under the Midwives Act 1966) Malaysia's statutory nursing regulator, established under the Nurses Act 1950 and the Nurses Registration Regulations 1985, operating under the Ministry of Health alongside the separate Malaysian Medical Council. Keeps and maintains the Register of Nurses; regulates nursing practice and training/examination procedures; issues registration credentials; enforces professional conduct standards through an established code of ethics. Nurses Act 1950; https://hq.moh.gov.my/nursing/en/about-us/midwives-board/
WPR Singapore Singapore Medical Council (SMC) Medicine A statutory board operating under the Ministry of Health, established under the Medical Registration Act 1997. Maintains the Register of Medical Practitioners; evaluates and recognizes international degrees; grants conditional or supervised practice; issues annual practicing certificates. Medical Registration Act 1997 (Chapter 174)
WPR Singapore Singapore Nursing Board (SNB) Nursing and midwifery, including Advanced Practice Nurses A statutory board established under the Nurses and Midwives Act 1999, operating under the Ministry of Health alongside the Singapore Medical Council. Approves or rejects applications for registration/enrolment of nurses and registration of midwives; issues and renews practising certificates; sets and maintains training, education, professional conduct and ethical standards; accredits nursing/midwifery education programmes; certifies Advanced Practice Nurses. Nurses and Midwives Act 1999; https://www.snb.gov.sg/who-we-are/functions-of-snb/
WPR Australia Medical Board of Australia (MBA) Medicine The statutory National Board responsible for regulating the medical profession in Australia, operating under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law (2009) as part of Ahpra's National Registration and Accreditation Scheme. Registers medical practitioners across multiple registration types (general, specialist, provisional, limited, non-practising, student); sets registration standards, codes, guidelines and CPD requirements; manages notifications/complaints; assesses overseas-trained doctors. Health Practitioner Regulation National Law Act 2009; https://www.medicalboard.gov.au/; https://www.ahpra.gov.au/
WPR Australia Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) Nursing and midwifery A statutory National Board established under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law, working in partnership with Ahpra. Registers practitioners and students; develops uniform national professional standards, codes, and guidelines; approves accredited programs of study. Health Practitioner Regulation National Law Act 2009
WPR New Zealand Medical Council of New Zealand (MCNZ) Medicine A statutory authority appointed and operating under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003. Registers medical practitioners; sets scopes of practice and competence standards; issues practicing certificates; reviews performance and fitness to practice. Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003
WPR New Zealand Nursing Council of New Zealand (NCNZ) Nursing New Zealand's statutory regulator for nursing, first established in 1902 (making New Zealand the first country to legally mandate nurse registration) and now operating under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003. Registers nurses and sets standards for nursing education, competence and practice; issues annual practising certificates; investigates fitness-to-practise concerns, in parallel with the Medical Council of New Zealand's equivalent role for doctors. Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nursing_Council_of_New_Zealand
